The generalized Gauss-Newton matrix is an approximation of the Hessian matrix that is highly dependent on the selected entry-point parameters, often resulting in parameter-dependent eigenvalues. This dependency can be problematic, as eigenvalues typically lack a clear low-dimensional structure. Our novel viewpoint, ViViT, reveals that this matrix does indeed possess a low-dimensional structure, with only r significant singular values and numerous zero singular values. The model parameters can be effectively optimized by focusing solely on the parameter subspace associated with these significant singular values, while the remaining parameters related to zero singular values can be disregarded. Our analysis also reveals that this subspace aligns with the tangent plane of the local trajectory at its endpoint, providing an explanation for curvature entry methods. Furthermore, this perspective enables the development of a computationally efficient optimization algorithm, significantly reducing complexity from cubic to quadratic, with a minimal dependency on the model's dimensions.

We examined the impact of grammatical gender on how words are represented in languages that assign gender to nouns, focusing on how frequently used gendered nouns affect this representation. Our investigation revealed that, in multilingual models where a single gender category applies to all nouns, different gendered variants of the same word are given distinct internal classifications. This distinction arises from the frequency of those gendered variants, with higher frequency variants being assigned a more dominant classification. Our results also show that, in languages with multiple gender categories, each category's internal representation is influenced by the frequency of nouns associated with that category. Our findings reveal that, in languages with three gender categories, one category's female designation is more broadly applicable, while the other two are more specific.

Groups derived from integer lattices of Hermitian forms over complex or real numbers in specific dimensions exhibit specific properties regarding discrete groups, including the relationship between finite presentation and uniqueness of irreducible components, as well as the characterization of when these groups have a finite presentation and a specific property known as "attractiveness" based on the number of variables in the underlying form.

This study presents an innovative approach to estimate object positions for categories not present in training data. We leverage existing object detectors and classifiers trained on vast datasets to propose a zero-shot positioning method for unfamiliar object classes. We formulate the challenge as a zero-shot detection task, where we utilize dataset-specific detectors to generate position predictions for unfamiliar object classes. We demonstrate that this approach outperforms baseline methods in both synthetic and real-world scenarios, achieving a mean average precision improvement of 12.8% and 10.3% respectively, while also achieving a high correlation of 0.88 in estimated versus actual object centroids.

Traffic forecasting is a crucial task for intelligent transportation systems, but the problem becomes more complex with extensive sparse data. Traditional methods often struggle to handle sparse data and similar patterns. This research proposes a novel approach that combines data similarity and uses an autoencoder to extract hidden features. The proposed method leverages the similarity between time periods and uses an autoencoder to fill in missing data. By incorporating these features, a long short-term memory network can more effectively predict future traffic. The proposed approach has shown significant improvements in prediction accuracy compared to traditional methods.

This study introduces a family of Variational Graph Autoencoders (VACA) that employs a graph-based generative model to represent complex data relationships. By leveraging a latent space, the VACA model enables the investigation of counterfactual and interventional questions. We demonstrate that the VACA model can be utilized to calculate closed-form interventions and counterfactuals. Furthermore, the VACA family incorporates a graph convolution module that facilitates the handling of non-iid features. Through simulations and real-world applications, the VACA model is shown to effectively address complex causal queries.

We've developed REALTA, a unique system designed to automatically detect, track, and manage radio transients in real-time using the LOFAR facility. This innovation allows for the prioritization of transient events and scheduling them for detailed observation. Initial results from REALTA's integration with LOFAR demonstrate its effectiveness, showcasing radio supernovae, changing sources, and radio transients that were previously unidentified. Our paper outlines the system's functionality, initial results, and discusses the potential scientific and technical benefits of REALTA.

A novel metastructure has been developed using a novel combination of dielectric and metallic nanorods, optimized through an AI-driven method to achieve enhanced properties in the terahertz spectrum. This metastructure, featuring nanorods of varying orientations, exhibits superior magnetic response characteristics compared to conventional metamaterials, with the ability to control the polarization of incident waves and produce a significant phase shift. Additionally, a novel AI-based method has been created to analyze and simulate complex metastructures, streamlining the design process and reducing computational costs.

The film industry is a vast and intricate network of interconnected elements,
with each component influencing others in complex and sometimes unpredictable
ways. Understanding how these elements interact is essential for making informed
decisions and maximizing profits. A film's success is not solely determined by
its artistic quality but is heavily reliant on external factors such as marketing,
distribution, and audience appeal. By analyzing the interplay between these
factors, researchers can uncover valuable insights into the industry's inner workings.
A new dataset has been developed to investigate how pre-release information
affects a film's potential earnings. This dataset includes information on over 10,000
films released between 1994 and 2019, along with their box office performance,
genre, runtime, and other relevant details. By applying machine learning techniques,
researchers can uncover hidden patterns and correlations within the dataset,
ultimately leading to more accurate predictions of a film's potential earnings.
This research has significant implications for the industry, as it provides a
framework for making informed decisions and maximizing profits.

A new auxiliary power demand is proposed to supplement the existing system's primary power requirement of maintaining system frequency at a setpoint.  The proposed demand is triggered only when the system's rate of frequency change surpasses a predetermined threshold.  This auxiliary demand acts to counteract the root cause of system frequency deviation, thereby providing an added layer of system protection.  In this paper, the proposed model of auxiliary frequency regulation is introduced and its effectiveness in mitigating voltage instability is demonstrated through simulation studies.

This research paper examines the importance of cyberphysical networks in systems that are rapidly evolving, emphasizing the need for the integration of intelligence at the core of these networks. By incorporating human cognition into the network's control systems, we can create more dynamic and efficient interactions between the network's cyber and physical components. The paper explores the potential benefits of this approach, including the development of self-healing, self-organizing, and self-optimizing networks, and discusses the challenges and opportunities associated with the design and implementation of cyberphysical networks with cognitive capabilities.

A notable 3-fold increase in emission intensity is observed in the ultraviolet and soft X-ray spectrum of blazars during their peak activity compared to their radio state, yet the origin of this phenomenon remains unclear. Our research employs a Monte Carlo code to simulate polarized light and its polarization patterns produced by particle interactions within non-uniform magnetic fields. We apply this method to investigate the polarization of non-uniform magnetic fields responsible for the UV/soft X-ray surplus in the spectra of blazars. Our findings indicate that such fields can generate the observed intensity and polarization patterns of the UV/soft X-ray surplus, with the polarization pattern being consistent with the observed levels of polarization in the corresponding BL Lac objects.

Recent breakthroughs in analytic extension over flat surfaces have significantly advanced our understanding across disciplines.  However,  a significant limitation remains in extending these methods to surfaces with intricate three-dimensional forms.  In this research,  we have developed a method for performing analytic extension over complex three-dimensional surfaces.  By utilizing a minimal surface that conforms to a given boundary,  we have created a framework that enables the embedding of a given set of points in a,  either maximally or holomorphically,  conformal manner.  This method has been successfully applied to a diverse range of three-dimensional objects,  including the human body,  and has been further validated through,  among other things,  shape matching and correspondence analysis.

We explore the detection capabilities of local measurements on composite quantum systems, specifically focusing on the problem of locally identifying pure global states with certain symmetries, such as those occurring in spin-singlet states, which remain unchanged under the exchange of any two subsystems, described mathematically as the antisymmetric subspace $\mathcal{H}_a$. Our key finding reveals that local measurements cannot effectively detect certain states within $\mathcal{H}_a$, particularly those that are pure but not accessible through the application of local measurements alone. This phenomenon is demonstrated by the fact that some symmetric pure states are not even detectable by the most basic local measurement, which is the check for the null vector, within $\mathcal{H}_a$. Moreover, we demonstrate that a comprehensive set of local measurements can only detect states within $\mathcal{H}_a$ that are not pure globally.

Baryon creation through the splintering of a QCD string is examined using quantum theory. Baryon density is influenced by QCD string helicity and temperature. Baryon distribution follows a quantized QCD string splintering model. Baryon distribution's parameters, including temperature and flow velocity, are determined experimentally.

The travel duration variation, a key indicator of the Sun's internal rotation rate, is influenced by the presence of electric currents. To explore this, we analyzed how the Sun's internal magnetic fields interact with its fluid motion, specifically focusing on the region near active areas. Using the Sun's observed rotation rate, we found that the presence of certain currents, such as those with a westward component, could significantly impact the travel duration rate. Specifically, we found that the presence of certain currents, such as those with a poloidal component, could significantly impact the travel duration rate. Additionally, we found that the presence of certain currents, such as those with a toroidal component, could significantly impact the travel duration rate.

The detection of gravitational waves has been hindered by their incredibly low amplitude, with current technology unable to identify waves even from the most intense supernovae occurring at the nearest distance of 10 kpc. We propose an alternative approach, involving a search for a Gravitational Wave Background, with a focus on detecting non-relativistic magnetic fields that could be influenced by a stochastic background within the frequency range of the Pulsar Timing Array. We outline the theoretical basis for this concept, discuss the implications of various stochastic sources, and provide the detection limits for magnetic field amplitude, with a specific emphasis on the continuous monitoring of the Galactic Center region, such as near Cassiopeia A, over a period of 10 years.

Light field (LF) technology has garnered significant attention due to its capacity to provide additional visual information. However, the high data requirements for storing and transmitting LF images pose a significant challenge. Traditional compression methods often neglect the spatial variability in LF images, leading to subpar performance. In response, deep learning-based approaches have been developed to improve compression efficiency. Nevertheless, these methods typically rely on computationally intensive operations, such as convolution and recurrent neural networks, which are impractical for real-world applications. In this research, a novel and efficient LF compression system is presented, leveraging spatial variability and employing learned-driven compression. By utilizing a 2D convolutional autoencoder to extract and represent the core content of the disparity map, the proposed system effectively captures the structural information of LF images. Moreover, the latent representation is efficiently compressed using low-complexity operations, such as quantization and entropy coding, which are suitable for real-time processing. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the proposed system's superior compression efficiency and remarkable visual quality, with notable advantages in terms of computational complexity and real-world applicability.

Cross-language information access is a crucial challenge in multilingual societies, and it is particularly significant for developing cross-language search capabilities in information systems. This research introduces a cross-language search method that integrates both interactive and non-interaction frameworks to improve retrieval quality. The proposed interactive search model leverages an initial non-interaction phase to establish a solid foundation, and then incorporates an interactive phase to refine search results through iterative query construction and refinement. A novel interactive query construction method is proposed to enhance precision, and experiments demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in achieving superior cross-language search performance.

In resource-limited settings such as Low and Middle Income Countries, accurately estimating the prevalence of chronic diseases in underrepresented areas is crucial. This study compares various statistical methods for producing reliable estimates within specific regions, including Bayesian hierarchical models, empirical Bayesian models, and small-area estimation models. We utilized data from the 2015/2016 Demographic and Health Survey in Malawi to calculate hypertension and diabetes rates across the country's districts. The results show that incorporating external information, like environmental factors, improves the accuracy of the estimates. Moreover, our analysis indicates that utilizing small-area estimation techniques yields more precise and reliable results compared to traditional survey estimates.

A novel approach to returning classical data in quantum computing experiments has been developed. Inspired by the "Kelly wagering" principle, this strategy ensures that the quantum state of the system accurately reflects the outcome of the program's execution. The data return method relies on a quantum channel that maps the final program state to a continuous variable, allowing for the retrieval of the outcome with a high degree of certainty. The approach has been successfully tested using the IBM Q Experience, demonstrating the feasibility of the method in practical quantum computing experiments.

The study of two-dimensional materials, specifically monolayer and bilayer compounds, has gained significant attention due to their unique properties. Researchers are particularly interested in the electronic properties of these materials, especially the alignment of quasiparticle energies and the formation of excitons. In this study, we investigate the electronic properties of 12 types of two-dimensional materials, including MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds, using first-principles calculations. Our results show that these materials have unique stacking-independent excitons and stacking-dependent quasiparticle energy alignments. Additionally, we found that excitons in these materials have unique characteristics, such as being indirect in some cases and having unique binding energies. Our study provides valuable insights into the electronic properties of these materials and their potential applications in future devices.

A search for the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay is conducted, and a statistical anomaly is observed in data, with significance reaching $4.2\sigma$. This discrepancy is not attributed to a single factor, but rather to an accumulation of unusual decay patterns. This phenomenon is investigated and its implications for understanding baryon decay processes are discussed.

The formation of a protoplanetary disk is a crucial step in creating a planetary system, but the exact process behind its creation remains unclear. To address this, researchers have developed a new model that simulates the formation of a disk from a collapsing molecular cloud core. The model, which uses a simplified representation of the core, shows how a disk develops when a specific type of instability occurs during the collapse. The model, which matches certain observations of young planetary systems, reveals that the formation of a disk is linked to the movement of material within the core. The results suggest that understanding the internal structure of clouds is essential for explaining the formation of planetary systems.

The optical behavior of our planet's atmosphere is crucial in astronomy, affecting observations both during the day and at night. To replicate this phenomenon in computer simulations, a detailed model is required that incorporates the unique properties of our atmosphere. A basic model is insufficient to capture the optical characteristics of our planet, so a more sophisticated model is developed and refined using real-world data. By comparing simulated images with real observations, the effectiveness of the new model is demonstrated and its parameters are optimized. This improved model is then used to simulate a star's visibility under different conditions, showcasing its potential applications in astronomy.

In many real-world scenarios, such as healthcare, finance, and retail, time series data is often characterized by irregular sampling intervals and the presence of missing values. This issue is particularly pronounced when dealing with temporal data, where traditional models often struggle to capture the underlying patterns and relationships. This paper addresses these challenges by developing a novel multi-term temporal sequence model that leverages the power of probabilistic programming to perform Bayesian variational inference. This innovative approach enables efficient handling of irregular time series data and missing values, while also providing a principled uncertainty quantification framework. Furthermore, the model incorporates a sparsity-inducing prior to promote parsimonious parameterization and improve interpretability. This results in a highly versatile and interpretable framework that outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both synthetic and real-world applications.

A deep and persistent problem in the study of topological groups revolves around the relationship between a group and its continuous functions, particularly the connection between original group structures and their associated dual representations, known as Pontryagin duals. The challenge lies in translating group structures into the domain of function spaces while preserving key properties. This line of inquiry has significant implications for understanding the limitations of reasoning in continuous domains, with applications extending beyond group theory to fields such as metric and order-based structures.

This research investigates the concept of differential confidentiality in the context of Federated Learning, a privacy-preserving technique. We introduce a metric called $k$-anonymity, which measures the difficulty of identifying a specific client's data from the server's model output. We demonstrate that when a client shares their information, their weight updates will inevitably leak, thereby compromising the system's confidentiality. To address this issue, we introduce a novel method, Local Differential Privacy, to obscure a client's weight updates, thereby safeguarding the server from potential data breaches. We also present a metric, the Privacy Loss Function, to quantify the impact of local differential privacy on the system's confidentiality. The findings indicate that local differential privacy can significantly mitigate data leakage, while also providing theoretical and empirical evidence that client participation is essential for achieving optimal model performance and privacy balance.

We propose a theoretical framework that combines supersymmetric extensions with additional $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetries and right-handed neutrinos, including those with right-handed Majorana properties. The introduction of these elements enables dark matter and dark energy to be explained within this framework. The dark matter candidate is a light sterile neutrino, whose properties can be tested by future experiments such as X-ray observations and particle colliders. The dark energy is attributed to the right-handed Majorana mass of the neutrino, which can be generated by a $U(1)_X$ Higgs field and a right-handed neutrino. The model's structure is then explored, including its implications for the $Z^\prime$ boson and dark matter detection, as well as its potential to be tested by future experiments.

In recent years, the integration of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) has garnered significant attention in the research community due to their potential to enhance wireless communication systems. However, the practical deployment of IRS systems is hindered by the challenge of accurately modeling the relationship between incoming and outgoing signals. This paper presents a solution to this problem by leveraging unsupervised learning methods to establish this relationship without requiring labeled data. The proposed approach utilizes a novel dataset generation technique that incorporates channel disruption to simulate real-world scenarios and improve model performance. The performance of this method is evaluated through numerical simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness in maximizing network throughput.

The study of the $^{186}$Hg isotope's properties and its role in the $\beta$-decay process is crucial for understanding the properties of neutron-rich mercury isotopes and the characteristics of single-neutron and double-neutron gaps. A new low-energy $\beta$-decay spectrum of $^{186}$Hg has been measured using a high-efficiency detector, revealing that its $\beta$-decay energy is lower than previously estimated. A spectrum of neutron-rich $^{186}$Hg was measured for the first time, and its characteristics were found to differ from theoretical predictions. A $\beta$-delayed neutron emission probability of 15.5% was determined, and these findings have significant implications for nuclear structure models and the study of exotic isotopes.

In a single, unified framework, we explore how gauge interactions influence both dark matter stability and the creation of matter in the universe. The simplest model of dark matter, composed of fermions, remains stable due to the influence of an $SU(2)_L$ gauge interaction. This interaction also enables dark matter to decay into standard model particles, such as a pair of leptons, which in turn can generate a baryon asymmetry in the universe. By comparing the matter imbalance in the universe to the dark matter density, we find that this process can explain the matter asymmetry in the universe and make predictions about the dark matter density and the dark matter's detection capabilities.

This study presents a new data-informed control approach that effectively manages complex systems with intricate dynamics, such as aircraft, even when data is scarce. The proposed method combines a key concept from reinforcement learning, known as the critic, with an optimization technique to quickly converge to a stable solution, despite limited data and the use of simplified models. The algorithm's success relies on incorporating information from supplementary sources, like expert knowledge, to improve model accuracy. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a challenging simulation of learning to fly a small aircraft, where it achieves remarkable results using data from just a few trials.

Ward identities in conformal quantum Toda theory serve as fundamental operator constraints, analogous to the energy-momentum tensor's role in conformal quantum field theory. Focusing on the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda model with unit central charge, this study derives the explicit form of the Ward current, a non-trivial outcome stemming from the conformal field's inherent complexity.

A connection network, a type of neural network, represents relationships between network nodes through edge weights. Recent advancements in applying connection networks to visual recognition have revealed their potential in modeling intricate visual patterns. However, their integration into unsupervised learning, particularly with Generative Adenversarial Networks, has remained a largely unexplored area. Our research introduces RelationGAN, a novel Generative ADversarial Network framework that utilizes connection networks to learn relational dependencies within data triplets. By leveraging their capacity to model complex visual patterns, RelationGAN achieves impressive results in unsupervised image representation learning and transfer learning, outperforming traditional convolutional neural network-based approaches.

The typical quantum key distribution protocol is the BB84 scheme, but its distance is restricted by the loss of optical fibers. A more recent method called the twin-field QKX has the potential to overcome this limitation by reaching distances of several hundred kilometers. A critical requirement for the QKX protocol is the synchronization of optical phase, which poses a significant technical challenge. In this study, we present a modified, phase-insensitive version of the twin-field QKX protocol that eliminates the need for phase synchronization. The experimental results show that this new protocol can be implemented using current technology, resulting in a successful exchange of cryptographic keys.

Let $\mathbb{B}_p$ be the bounded type-$p$ Fock domain in the $l^2(\mathbb{Z}_+^d)$ Hilbert space, where $1\leq p<\infty$, and let $\mathbb{B}_{2}$ be the Bergman disk, where we investigate the Toeplitz algebras generated by the Toeplitz operators $S_\varphi$ with continuous symbols $\varphi$ on $\mathbb{B}_{p}$ and $\mathbb{B}_{2}$, respectively. Our findings reveal that the C*-algebras generated by these operators are isomorphic, established by demonstrating that each algebra contains a copy of the other, thereby creating mutual inclusions.

This research focuses on developing an efficient method for identifying everyday items in images, specifically targeting open-ended object detection. A novel approach is proposed that utilizes bounding-box annotations derived from human-object interaction data to train a model capable of recognizing a vast array of objects without predefined categories. The model's performance is evaluated on an image dataset comprising 1,000 categories and demonstrates its capability to generalize well to 3,000 additional categories without any model retraining. The model's success is attributed to its ability to leverage weak annotations and its use of advanced techniques such as feature enhancement and multi-scale detection.

The Rho Ophiuchus cloud core is home to a complex and dynamic region of gas formation, featuring the L1688 subcloud, which hosts the Class 0 protostar S1. Utilizing high-resolution millimeter and submillimeter observations, we mapped out the distribution of various gas components within L1688, which includes ionized gas, carbon monoxide, and other molecular species. Our analysis reveals that the L1688 subcloud, which spans approximately 1000 astronomical units, is characterized by a narrow, cone-shaped region of gas formation extending away from S1. Within this area, we observed distinct patterns of gas formation, which can be attributed to the influence of external factors such as radiation and magnetic fields. Our findings suggest that the L1688 subcloud, which spans approximately 1000 astronomical units, is characterized by a narrow, cone-shaped region of gas formation extending away from S1.

The success of Vision Transformers in computer vision has been driven by their unique self-attention mechanism, which has enabled breakthroughs in various applications. A significant advantage of Transformers over traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) is their ability to capture long-range dependencies and global context, leading to improved performance in complex tasks. Despite their promising results, researchers are still exploring ways to adapt Transformers for use in computer vision. This paper provides a comprehensive review of Transformers in computer vision, covering their core components, data preprocessing, network architecture, and post-processing. Additionally, we examine existing variants of Transformers, their applications, and future research directions, aiming to shed light on the strengths and weaknesses of Transformers in computer vision and guide future research efforts.

This research investigates the use of latent factor models for forecasting mortality rates, comparing two factor models - one that incorporates time-sensitive factor loadings and another with fixed factor loadings. The latent factor's ability to capture temporal changes in mortality rates is explored, with a specific focus on the effects of major historical events such as the two World Wars and the AIDS epidemic on US mortality rates across different age groups and causes of death. The study compares the predictive accuracy of the factor models with traditional mortality prediction models using data from the US and the UN. The results reveal that the factor models outperform the traditional models in most cases, with a latent factor that effectively reflects significant historical events. The research also indicates the presence of a common factor shared across different causes of death within the same time period, with some unique factors specific to certain causes of death.

In Neural Architecture Exploration (NAX), minor modifications to an existing neural network architecture can lead to significant performance disparities, thereby making it challenging to pinpoint the optimal solution. To mitigate this issue, we introduce the concept of "disruption" to quantify the extent to which an update to an architecture affects its performance, and subsequently, we propose three techniques to minimize the impact of this disruption, including: (1) evaluating multiple samples of the baseline to establish a more reliable reference point; (2) analyzing the structural components of the baseline to inform the exploration process; and (3) developing a novel metric to assess the similarity between the baseline and updated search spaces. Our experiments demonstrate that these strategies can substantially reduce disruption and, as a result, enhance NAX performance.

This research introduces an open-source R library, theft, which facilitates the evaluation of data series through statistical analysis. The theft.R package offers a comprehensive set of functions to compute various statistical measures, such as mean, variance, and standard deviation, as well as more complex metrics like coefficient of variation, Attenbrow's V, and root mean squared error. These statistical examinations can be visually represented in bar charts, heatmaps, or directed graphs. The theft package is demonstrated with two datasets: the well-known Abalone dataset and a custom-generated time series.

We demonstrate the existence of complete CAT(0) spaces that exclude geodesic triangles with angles of $\pi/3$ for each corner. This finding has significant implications in the study of non-positive curvature. Specifically, it indicates the impossibility of extending the definition of non-positive curvature from geodesically complete CAT(0) spaces to non-convex subspaces, even if those subspaces consist of a single geodesic triangle and have a complete CAT(0) ambient space.

This study introduces a novel Bayesian approach to assessing the reliability of translators, evaluating the quality of machine translations in terms of their human translator's proficiency. The proposed model accounts for varying levels of translator expertise and their impact on translation quality, enabling the assessment of specific translators' reliability in terms of their translation error rates, regardless of their expertise. The approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through evaluation using a publicly available dataset of machine translations, carried out by translators with diverse levels of proficiency.

The Landau-Bethe-Salpeter equation, which models the response of a system to light, has solutions that describe how energy is absorbed in different directions. These solutions are called eigenvalues and eigenvectors. A new set of sum rules has been developed for these eigenvalues and found to connect with existing principles in the field of optical science. These sum rules show that the sum of certain quantities related to these eigenvalues equals fundamental properties of a material, which can be understood through the material's optical properties.

Deep neural networks, particularly those with fully connected links, have proven effective in processing data, but their complexity and inefficiency make them impractical for real-world applications. This study investigates the effectiveness of pruning, a technique that removes redundant connections, on fully connected networks compared to their fully linked counterparts. By applying this method, we found that fully connected networks perform comparably to their fully linked counterparts, thus suggesting that fully connected networks are sufficient for many practical purposes. This finding has significant implications for the development of more efficient and scalable machine learning models.

In many countries, purchasing a lottery ticket is the most popular form of gambling.
This study examines the highest anticipated value of a lottery ticket from a consumer's perspective.
We develop a method to determine the optimal parameters of a lottery ticket that maximizes its anticipated value.
The value of a lottery ticket depends on the number of drawn numbers, the total numbers available, and the number of candidates who purchase tickets.
To maximize the anticipated value, lottery organizers should limit the number of drawn numbers, total numbers available, and ticket purchasers.
To achieve this, the lottery organizer should set ticket prices to ensure that consumers' utility from non-monetary sources equals their anticipated monetary utility.
This strategy ensures that the maximum anticipated value of a lottery ticket is maintained.
The model is then applied to the French lottery "EuroMillions" to analyze the results.

The method developed by V. D. Skakiev and A. V. Pankov for calculating multi-loop anomalous dimensions of the $\phi^Q$ operator is presented, along with calculations of its six-loop "unusual" dimension at large $N$ in the $O(N)$ model.

This study presents a theoretical framework for simulating valley coherence in electron-phonon systems, enabling the evaluation of how various interaction mechanisms affect valley relaxation. By developing a multi-mechanism framework, the effect of novel electron-phonon interactions on valley dynamics is examined, specifically in graphene and related materials, as well as in transition metal dichalcogenides. Our analysis reveals that the novel interaction mechanism can significantly extend valley lifetimes, with the potential to improve detection efficiency in valleytronics applications.

The proposed approach successfully addresses the challenge of cross-domain adjustment by first applying a two-stage approach to handle the differences in visual domains. In the initial stage, domain-specific features are extracted and adapted. Subsequently, a unified representation is achieved through a domain-invariant module. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through a series of experiments on a variety of visual tasks.

The widespread adoption of deep learning has led to the development of numerous state-of-the-art models, with a primary focus on vector representations. However, there are cases where spherical representations are more beneficial, particularly in fields such as computer vision, natural language processing, and recommendation systems. This paper introduces a novel variant of the t-SNE algorithm, dubbed VMF-SNE, which leverages the properties of the von Mises-Fisher distribution to learn spherical embeddings. By relaxing the assumption of Gaussian data, VMF-SNE enables more accurate modeling of non-linearly related data points. Furthermore, VMF-SNE is shown to be more robust to noise and outliers compared to its traditional counterpart.

The research examines the relationship between the energy of a polaron and the interactions of a dual-dimensional Fermi gas using a Monte Carlo approach based on diagrammatic methods. By exploring the connection between the parameters of the diagrams and the corresponding Monte Carlo weights, a scaling law is proposed that can be used to estimate the parameters for higher-order diagrams. Furthermore, by leveraging the knowledge of the parameters, a model is developed to investigate the behavior of the polaron in the strong-coupling regime. The results of the research align with previous findings from Monte Carlo and diagrammatic methods, and open new avenues for investigating polaron physics.

We introduce a hybrid digital-analog method to model fermionic systems on quantum computers by transforming quantum emulation into a circuit-based representation. This approach enables the use of native qubit operations to simulate complex interactions. We apply this digital-analog method to simulate a one-dimensional Hubbard model with quantum computers, achieving accurate results that surpass classical computational limits. This breakthrough demonstrates the potential of quantum emulation in exploring complex physical systems, even in the presence of quantum computational limitations.

We investigate the asymptotic behavior of a specific set of polynomial sequences derived from a particular type of graph labelings, which are related to a widely studied family of graphs. Our analysis yields closed-form expressions for these sequences, allowing us to establish a generating function for them. Additionally, we establish a recurrence relation that defines the growth of these sequences in terms of the graph's order.

We present a geometric interpretation for the Hitchin fibration within the context of the Veech arc space, utilizing the concept of graded parabolic representations in SL_3(C). This fibration forms an integral part of the broader investigation into the representation varieties associated with the fundamental group of the punctured torus, T. Building upon prior studies, we demonstrate that the abelian varieties resulting from the Hitchin fibration are inherently linked to the Arf invariants found in one-cycles on the Riemann surface, S, which is obtained by collapsing the arcs defining the Veech surface, V. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the representation varieties, R, and the corresponding projective varieties, P. This equivalence holds for a substantial subset of the representation varieties, which is determined by the Arf invariants in one-cycles on the surface, S.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread remote work disruptions, prompting researchers to investigate how this shift impacts project success in software development. Focusing on the effectiveness of Scrum methodology, this study aims to uncover the specific effects of remote work on Scrum project outcomes. Through a comprehensive analysis involving multiple studies, we identified key factors influencing project achievement, including team size, project complexity, and communication effectiveness. The results reveal that remote work significantly alters project dynamics, emphasizing the need for tailored Scrum practices in distributed teams. The findings contribute to the existing body of knowledge and offer practical guidance for managing Scrum projects remotely.

The Gau-Wu value of a nonnegative, irreducible matrix with zero rows and columns sums is defined as the greatest value of x such that the matrix raised to the rth power is strictly greater than x times a specific matrix, where that specific matrix has the original matrix's zero rows and columns replaced with zero vectors of appropriate length. This study derives the Gau-Wu value for an arrowhead matrix of size 4 and examines the Gau-Wu value of a particular subset of nonnegative, irreducible matrices of size 4.

Measurements of electrons originating from the decay of beauty-hadons have been analyzed in ultra-central Pb-Pb collisions at a specific energy level. The electrons' elliptic motion was measured across various collision energies, revealing a pattern that was compared to theoretical predictions. Additionally, this measurement was correlated with the transverse momentum of the electrons, showing a distinct trend compared to previous measurements.

In our research, we investigate the relationship between the persistence diagrams of a specific type of alpha complex constructed from points of varying colors and the underlying persistence diagram of the points' spatial distribution. We discover that the persistence diagrams share a significant number of shared features, with the number of shared features being directly proportional to the number of distinct colors used. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the distance between the persistence diagrams can be described as a linear combination of the distances resulting from discarding the most and least reliable features, respectively.

This research investigates the interference channel's power control, specifically looking at how much better optimal power control performs in comparison to binary power control. We find that for a certain number of users, the gain of optimal power control over binary power control is significant and scales as the square root of the number of users. To prove this, we establish a lower bound that shows binary power control's limitations, and we also develop a sophisticated optimal power control strategy that achieves this result. This strategy is a linear combination of a set of vectors, and we show that it's possible to achieve significant performance improvements over binary power control by using it.

This research introduces a novel framework for auditing that integrates the Formal Concept Analysis lattice and Dempster-Shafer Theory to accommodate uncertain and incomplete data. The proposed approach is adaptable and can be applied to various auditing scenarios, such as evaluating management's financial projections, assessing a company's going concern status, or predicting the risk of business failure. To address the issue of incomplete information, we employ the Dempster-Shafer Theory for uncertainty management. The intersection of these two frameworks yields a context where objects and concepts are equipped with belief and plausibility functions, allowing for the measurement of an object's affinity with a concept. The distribution of affinity among the available knowledge base enables us to infer the affinity of an object with a concept. The proposed auditing framework is divided into two main components: formal concept analysis for auditing and uncertain auditing using Dempster-Shafer Theory. By combining these components, we obtain a flexible auditing system capable of handling diverse data and uncertainty.

The Strauss-Poisson process, first introduced in 1967, is a marked point process that generates random points within a specific region. This process is defined by a specified intensity and a user-defined function that determines the likelihood of points being present at any given location. This function can be negative, reflecting the idea of a "repulsive function" that prevents points from clustering together. This paper presents a new approach to creating Strauss processes that use a user-defined function that may not be strictly repulsive, and it also introduces a practical way of implementing Strauss processes with complex functions by using basic models and combining them through a technique known as "stitching."

A novel approach to quantifying the generalization of the ambiguity principle for spatial conversion has been developed, incorporating principles from both thermodynamics and information theory. Initially, this concept was applied within the context of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, where it was found to be equivalent to minimizing thermodynamic free energy. Subsequently, this concept was extended to spatial conversions under Lorentz and Galilean transformations, where it was found that the generalized ambiguity principle can be expressed as a function of the source and destination coordinates, velocities, and the associated momentum. Furthermore, this concept was applied to the study of the Tully-Fisher relation, where it was found that the generalized ambiguity principle can be expressed as a function of the source and destination coordinates, velocity, and the associated angular momentum. Ultimately, this concept was used to derive a universal relationship between the angular momentum and the mass of galaxies, independent of the specific model used to describe galaxy formation and evolution.

Multitasking is widely used in computer systems to efficiently utilize resources and achieve high system throughput. Typically, system software manages this process by dividing tasks and executing them concurrently, either by switching tasks or executing multiple tasks simultaneously. The former requires context switching, which can lead to performance degradation, while the latter demands multiple processing units. To leverage a single processing unit, current system software employs context switching, which causes tasks to frequently interrupt each other, resulting in the performance loss known as the "cache effect." To mitigate this, we propose a new approach that shares the processing unit among multiple tasks, combining elements of context switching and parallel processing. By doing so, we minimize the impact of the cache effect, improve multitasking performance, and reduce the complexity of system software. Our performance model quantifies the optimal number of tasks that can be run on a single processing unit, taking into account the overhead of system software and the impact of the cache effect.

A novel simulation approach is developed for a monopod robot capable of leaping on deformable terrain. The monopod model is based on a single rigid body with one actuated hinge, while the ground is simulated using a network of interconnected particles. The leaping motion is achieved through a combination of actuated jumps and passive adaptations to slow down the monopod. The proposed simulation method is then optimized using reinforcement learning to enable successful leaping on varied terrain conditions. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the new approach in achieving stable monopod leaps on both simulated and real-world yielding terrain.

A critical aspect of maintaining an in-demand service is ensuring smooth upgrades of the underlying software. This paper explores the complexities of upgrading large-scale IoT networks, where devices communicate over a mesh network and run specialized edge software. We discovered that even minor modifications to the edge software can result in substantial changes to the network's traffic patterns, causing prolonged periods of reduced throughput and increased latency. To address this challenge, we developed a new strategy for upgrading large-scale IoT networks, which minimizes disruptions to network traffic and reduces downtime. Our approach was tested on a large-scale mesh network, and the results demonstrated that it successfully reduced the negative impact of the upgrade process, significantly improving user experience and reducing the risk of upgrade failures.

We've investigated the transition of multifractal propagator exponents in a disordered quantum spin chain as it shifts from localized to thermal states. Our analysis revealed that a key propagator exponent undergoes a distinct phase transition at the point of localization, displaying universal behavior that mirrors the well-studied behavior near quantum phase transitions. This universal scaling is governed by a dynamic length scale, known as the Fock space propagator length, which diverges as the system approaches the localization transition. Our results shed new light on the nature of multifractality in fully quantum systems and its behavior across the localization transition.

We examine an interactive exploration problem where a target communicates with indistinguishable agents through wireless signals. The target contains numerous important data that need to be collected within a set time frame. Each agent has a limited storage capacity and can only hold one message at a time, but can create and destroy data. The target has a total exploration cost limit and seeks to find an optimal strategy to minimize the time required to gather all data. The target's optimal strategy is equivalent to solving a maximum flow problem in a time-invariant network, and we present a method for solving this problem when agents' movement is limited to grid spaces. Additionally, we propose an extension of this problem where agents' movement is not restricted to grid spaces.

In the realm of machine learning, the concept of adversarial examples has garnered significant attention, yet their counterparts in quantum computing remain underexplored. This study delves into the properties of global adversarial examples within quantum classifiers, revealing that they are inherently tied to disturbances rather than specific input states. Furthermore, it's been demonstrated that these disturbances exhibit invariance across different data manifolds, regardless of their dimensionality. A novel approach to constructing global adversarial examples is also proposed, along with an investigation into their utility in data denoising and classification tasks.

We investigate Steklov eigenvalues on two types of regions: those with spherical symmetry and those that deviate slightly from spherical symmetry. Firstly, we prove that for spherical shells, the Steklov spectrum consists of repeated integer values and is the same as the spherical Laplacian spectrum above a certain point. We then use this result to show that Steklov eigenvalues are consistent for regions that are closely approximated by spherical shells. Lastly, we discuss the behavior of Steklov eigenvalues in thin domains and their relationship with the geometry of the domain's boundary.

This study introduces novel methods for aligning and comparing sequences of actions, specifically infix and postfix alignments, which go beyond traditional full and prefix alignments by allowing for more flexible matching of action traces. Infix alignment identifies the longest continuous segment of two action sequences that are mutually comparable, while prefix alignment focuses on matching the initial sequence segment. To facilitate these comparisons, we introduce an infix and postfix alignment tool that employs dynamic programming to determine the optimal alignment score and path, which can be utilized in conformance checking and other data analysis tasks.

In wireless telecommunications, accurately predicting signal strength is a critical task that underpins various network functions. This paper focuses on developing a deep learning solution to model urban indoor and outdoor signal strength. Leveraging publicly available Google Maps and Tiago's datasets, we evaluate our model's ability to replicate the widely-used CST-ISA standard. Experimental results demonstrate that convolutional neural networks can effectively model and forecast signal strength, even with limited data. This capability positions these models as a potential replacement for computationally intensive and time-consuming traditional signal propagation models.

Our research defines and validates the Outperform algorithm, which is designed to find optimal solutions within out-of-sample cost models used in temporal planning. By formally verifying the algorithm's correctness, we ensure it can be applied to a wide range of complex cost models, unlike traditional models that are limited to specific, fixed cost structures. The process of verifying the algorithm involves using a combination of mathematical reasoning and model checking to confirm its correctness. The outcome of our work is a sound and complete Outperform* algorithm, which can be used to find optimal solutions within temporal planning problems. Additionally, we have developed a model-checker to rigorously validate whether the solutions generated by the Outperform algorithm are indeed optimal.

Energy growth models are a key component of climate change research, and their results are often used to inform policy. These models are typically simplified to make them more accessible, but this simplicity can hide significant model uncertainties. In this study, we examine energy growth models by examining their sensitivity to model simplifications. We examine four energy models, including three that are open-source models and one policy-based model. We find that these models are sensitive to model simplifications, and this has implications for climate change research. We suggest that future research should focus on reducing model simplifications to minimize uncertainty.

This paper investigates the global existence and uniqueness of solutions to the Vlasov-Poisson system within a three-dimensional bounded domain with a given initial condition and boundary condition. It considers two types of boundary conditions - a dynamic one and a static one. The study demonstrates that for a dynamic boundary condition, a solution can be obtained by extending the problem to an entire space, whereas for a static boundary condition, solutions can be obtained using a unique extension of the initial condition to an entire space.

This study introduces STRICT, a search engine query suggestion system that identifies the concept placement position within ambiguous search inputs. The majority of existing search engine query suggestion systems are trained on datasets that are relatively small and limited in scope. In contrast, STRICT leverages large search engine query logs to enhance its performance, thereby outdoing existing systems. The approach utilizes both supervised and unsupervised learning methods to accomplish its goal.

The development of smart materials capable of responding to external stimuli is highly sought after. Colloidal gels, characterized by a solid-like structure and complex internal organization, are promising candidates for creating responsive materials. When subjected to an intense ultrasonic field, gels exhibit a remarkable transformation in their physical properties. The application of ultrasound causes the gel to temporarily transition into a liquid state, and the process can be controlled by adjusting the sound wave's intensity and frequency. This phenomenon is attributed to the acoustic radiation forces acting on the gel's internal components, which overcome the weak inter-particle bonds holding the gel together. The ultrasound-induced movement of the gel's internal structure leads to the alignment of its organization, giving rise to an acoustic gel with unique and tunable properties. The acoustic gel's mechanical characteristics can be adjusted by manipulating the ultrasound parameters, and the gel's flow properties can also be influenced by this process. This development opens up new possibilities for creating responsive materials and has potential applications in various fields, including the development of 3D printing inks and other advanced material systems.

The Collatz Conjecture poses a straightforward procedure: given a natural number 'n', if 'n' is even, divide it by two; if 'n' is odd, multiply it by three and add one. Repeat this process with the resulting number. Although simple, the conjecture asserts that no matter the starting number, the sequence will eventually return to one. This paper explores various aspects of the conjecture, including proof by induction, graphical analysis, and data examination, and also discusses related phenomena and potential connections to broader mathematical concepts.

The rapid expansion of digital knowledge in STEM fields necessitates effective content management and organization. However, current categorization methods are inadequate, particularly when applied to complex, information-rich academic papers. To address this gap, our study proposes an innovative approach that leverages the crucial entities within individual papers to refine its subject categorization. By developing a novel neural network architecture that captures the relationships between these entities, our model outperforms the existing baseline in accurately identifying paper categories. Our findings indicate that the integration of neural architecture with entity information significantly enhances categorization accuracy.

In a matching process, two agents with ordinal preferences over each other's offerings engage in a negotiation. Each offering has a specific cost associated with it. The agent starts with an empty set of offerings and can only add to it, but can only accept offers that are better than what they already have. The goal is to determine the best strategy for agents to maximize their chances of a match, and we find that this strategy involves a type of threshold-based decision-making. Furthermore, we find that agents should consider making multiple offers to increase their chances of a match, and we find that this decision is influenced by the agents' costs and the current state of the negotiation.

To evaluate a summary's quality, a comprehensive and well-defined assessment metric is crucial. Traditional, element-wise comparison methods are often inadequate due to their inability to compare whole summaries effectively. A novel approach, SummScore, employs a Cross-Encoder model to compare summaries and source texts simultaneously, introducing a unique scoring mechanism. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that SummScore outperforms existing alternatives in various scenarios, including automated and human evaluations across multiple datasets, and also showcase its versatility in guiding summary improvement through self-correction.

In the field of computational imaging, capturing weak signals like those from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or ptychography, researchers often use detectors with quadratic sensitivity. This sensitivity can lead to errors in the reconstructed signals if not properly addressed. A recent method for solving this issue was proposed in a paper presented at the 2022 IEEE International Conference on Image Processing, where the authors developed an optimization-based approach to recover lost information. This method was found to be equivalent to solving a mathematical equation that describes how the observed signal relates to the original signal. By leveraging this connection, the authors created an efficient algorithm that can accurately recover the original signal, even when it is obscured by noise.

In the realm of autonomous vehicles, the fusion of perception data is a pivotal area of study, with recent research focusing on combining visual and localization data. However, the fusion of vision and vehicle movement data has received less attention. This study proposes a new method for integrating vertical feature detection from LiDAR scans with vehicle movement data to enhance the accuracy of features extracted from LiDAR scans. The approach, named BEVFusion, is built upon the backbone of a four-dimensional vehicle movement model and the transformer-based architecture of Deformable DETR, with the addition of a specialized module to refine vertical features. The method is designed to be versatile and can be seamlessly integrated with various LiDAR point cloud processing techniques.

In a simulated three-dimensional liquid turbulence, a sudden introduction of entropy occurs within an infinitesimally small area, causing thermal disturbance. This disturbance spreads and affects the surrounding flow, leading to a complex interaction between the thermal disturbance and the intense velocity fluctuations. Our research reveals that thermal disturbance behaves in a manner similar to velocity fluctuations, with both undergoing a process of cascade spreading across various scales. Furthermore, we observe a distinct relationship between temperature fluctuations and the characteristics of the range of dissipation, characterized by a universal scaling behavior. Our findings suggest that the thermal disturbance plays a crucial role in the development of scale-dependent phenomena observed in the range of dissipation, with potential implications for understanding fine-scale properties of heat transport in liquid turbulence.

The formation of periodic structures in a liquid, triggered by multiple self-induced diffraction effects, is extensively studied using both experimental and theoretical approaches. This study presents a detailed numerical analysis of the thermal profile generated by a laser in a liquid, which plays a pivotal role in the formation of these periodic structures. The findings of this study align with the experimental observations, providing a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving the complex thermal profile and periodic structure formation.

In the software engineering field, there's a growing interest in using natural language to document design information, which can be automatically mined to assist with design decisions. A notable approach involves utilizing topic models to uncover latent design entities and topics from such documentation. However, topic models can be sensitive to the order in which the data is presented, leading to variations in the information they uncover. To address this issue, we introduce the Conceptual Conclusion Stability (CCS) metric, which measures how consistent a topic model is across different orderings of the documentation. A lower CCS value indicates a more reliable topic model that uncovers stable concepts. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of CCS in guiding the development of a new topic model, which shows improved convergence and better performance in recovering design information compared to existing models.

The increasing availability of data streaming services has led to a surge in data analytics services, enabling businesses to gain insights from data streams in real-time. However, the rapid growth of data streams has made it increasingly difficult for users to process and analyze them using traditional streaming analytics pipelines. These pipelines are typically designed for smaller data streams and struggle to scale up to accommodate larger volumes of data. As a result, users are left with limited options for data access and analysis. To address this issue, we have developed a new data streaming architecture called H-STREAM, which enables users to build and run scalable streaming analytics pipelines that can efficiently process and analyze large volumes of data streams.

The production of heavy $t^\prime$ and $b^\prime$ associates in the $pp \rightarrow t^\prime b^\prime Q \bar{Q}$ channel is considered, where $Q$ and $\bar{Q}$ can be top or bottom quarks. This process is analyzed in the context of the $pp \rightarrow t^\prime b^\prime t \bar{t}$ reaction, highlighting two non-resonant production mechanisms that contribute significantly to five-body cross-sections. The first mechanism, $pp \rightarrow t^\prime b^\prime t \bar{t} X$, involves the production of a $t^\prime b^\prime$ pair and a $t \bar{t}$ pair, followed by the radiative emission of $X$ from a $W$ boson. The second mechanism, $pp \rightarrow t^\prime b^\prime t \bar{t} X$, involves the production of a $t^\prime b^\prime$ pair and a $t \bar{t}$ pair, followed by the radiative emission of $X$ from a $W$ boson. The study finds that these production mechanisms can significantly impact top and bottom associate cross-sections, with the $pp \rightarrow t^\prime b^\prime t \bar{t}$ reaction yielding a cross-section of approximately 10 fb at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. Knowledge graphs facilitate complex reasoning tasks in knowledge-aware NLP.
However, translating these graphs to different languages poses difficulties due to their large size and intricate structure.
To mitigate this challenge, we suggest using query replications to break down complex tasks into manageable parts.
By replying to each component separately, we can integrate the outcomes to generate a final result.
In this research, we apply this replication concept to address a challenging NLP task: machine translating SPARQL.
Our approach, which leverages parallel processing, demonstrates that our model outperforms a traditional single-head transformer on two datasets.
Additionally, we assess the effectiveness of our approach on managing diverse knowledge components, such as handling varying levels of complexity in knowledge graph queries.

This research investigates how researchers' reputation can be gauged based on their conference venue choices, utilizing the Venue Insights framework. By examining a dataset comprising 1.5 million computer science researchers and 7.5 million publications, we assess the reputation of the top 30 conferences and create a reputation metric for individual researchers. Our analysis explores the factors influencing researchers' venue selection, reveals patterns in their venue associations, and discovers that Venue Insights offers a superior evaluation of research impact, particularly for authors associated with top-tier conferences, top papers, and single-authored publications.

This study examines the role of artificial intelligence in regulatory frameworks, with a particular focus on the regulatory treatment of neural networks. The report begins by exploring the advantages and disadvantages of substituting the regulatory process with automated systems, before delving into a comparative analysis of how existing regulations apply to different types of artificial intelligence, including neural networks, in the contexts of market regulation and intellectual property. The assessment also considers the existing risk-based approaches and their applicability to neural networks, ultimately recommending the development of a new regulatory framework specifically designed to address the unique characteristics of these systems.

We have developed a novel hierarchical clustering method called Functorial
Hierarchical Grouping with Overlaps (FHGO) that utilizes a simplicial complex
to create clusters. FHGO is an unsupervised algorithm that generates a
multi-objective optimization problem consisting of two goals: minimizing the
similarity within groups and preventing overlap between them. By applying
Pareto optimality to this problem, FHGO produces a comprehensive hierarchical
clustering tree. A key feature of FHGO is its ability to create a functor from
the data space to the simplex space, allowing for the identification of
distinct, non-overlapping clusters at various levels of the hierarchy. FHGO
has been tested on both artificial and real-world datasets, including
brain scan images, and has shown superior performance compared to existing
clustering methods.

We introduce a cutting-edge, efficient method for retrieving visual data from streaming sources by focusing on short video segments. To tackle challenges posed by limited data availability and limited information within these segments, we propose a novel patch monitoring system that highlights the most valuable segments for restoration. Building on this framework, a streaming tensor ring model is developed to reconstruct visual data with limited pixels. This model is further enhanced with a multi-scale patch learning approach to capture broader spatial context and improve restoration quality. The proposed method achieves a balance between high performance and low computational demands, outperforming state-of-the-art techniques in restoration quality and video understanding tasks.

This part (II) of the (II) series focuses on Nichols algebras associated with conventional Weyl groups. A key finding here is the identification of all finite-dimensional Nichols algebras, which turns out to be a collection of homogeneous quantum linear spaces. These discoveries build upon previous work presented in Part 1, expanding the analysis to include rank 3 cases not previously explored.

A recent breakthrough in theoretical physics has established a specific power spectrum for chaotic motions driven by inertial waves in deep fluids with strong turbulence. This development provides a more accurate model for understanding wave turbulence and its impact on sound wave propagation and heat transfer. The theoretical model was built upon earlier research, including the discovery of an inverse energy cascade and the prediction of a specific energy spectrum. To further validate these theories, researchers employed advanced numerical simulations of turbulent flows, employing high-resolution methods and sophisticated algorithms. The simulations, which involved detailed analyses of fluid motion and wave behavior, provided compelling evidence supporting the predicted power spectrum and its characteristics.

This study focuses on determining the maximum weight autonomous set within a graph, where each edge has an associated positive weight. An autonomous set is defined as a subset that contains the source of every possible path within the graph. To achieve this objective, we present a revised version of the algorithm proposed by Dahlhaus et al., which was previously demonstrated to be equivalent in complexity to finding a minimum feedback vertex set in a directed graph. The revised algorithm, known as IGA, is shown here to compute the same autonomous set as the original, but with significantly improved computational efficiency. Furthermore, we show that IGA can be executed in O(m + n) time, in addition to providing an alternative linear-time algorithm for computing a minimum feedback vertex set in certain classes of directed graphs.

This study investigates the thermodynamic properties of monolayer graphene through an applied electric field, utilizing a comprehensive Hamiltonian that integrates electric field effects, deformations, and electron interactions. By applying the Dicke model and employing the mean-field approximation, the research delves into the thermal stability of electric field-modified graphene and its electronic phase transitions. The study's key findings reveal that electric field adjustments can induce structural phase transitions, stabilize trigonal distortion, and stabilize electron carriers. The research also demonstrates that electric field adjustments can modify electron and phonon temperature dependencies, broaden the Dirac fermion Fermi surface, and enhance electron-phonon coupling strength. The study concludes that electric field adjustments have the potential to improve thermal conductivity in graphene.
